answer: Korea (Republic of Korea) has the highest GNI per capita at the right endpoint in Figure O.5, at about 32,000 constant 2015 US$, above Chile (~16,500) and Poland (~13,000–14,000) in 2022. [wdr-p040-chart-00-000]
question: In Figure O.5, which of Korea, Poland and Chile has the highest GNI per capita at the right endpoint?

events.query: Figure O.5 Korea Poland Chile GNI per capita right endpoint

results.text:
Figure O.5
Line chart titled: "In the Republic of Korea, Poland, and Chile, the rapid growth from middle- to high-income status has been interspersed with economic crises." X-axis: years 1960 to 2022 (tick marks shown at regular intervals, labels rotated). Y-axis: "GNI per capita (constant 2015 US$)" from 0 to 35,000. Three country series are shown: Korea, Rep. (dark blue/black line) rising from about 1,000 in 1960 to about 32,000 in 2022, with a noticeable dip/slowdown around the late 1990s and then continued growth; Poland (orange line) starting around 3,000 in 1960, rising gradually with a dip in the early 1980s, then increasing to about 13,000–14,000 by 2022 with a small dip around 2020; Chile (teal line) visible from the mid-1990s onward, rising from about 5,500 to about 16,500 by 2022, with a slight dip around 2020. Three dotted horizontal income-threshold reference lines are labeled within the plot: "LMIC threshold" near the bottom, "UMIC threshold" around the mid-lower range, and "HIC threshold" around the upper-middle range. Country names are printed near the right ends of the corresponding lines. Source note below the chart: "Source: WDR 2024 team using WDI (World Development Indicators) (Data Catalog), World Bank, Washington, DC, https://datacatalog.worldbank.org/search/dataset/0037712." Note: "GNI = gross national income; HIC = high-income country; LMIC = lower-middle-income country; UMIC = upper-middle-income country."

Figure O.1
Title: "Income per capita of middle-income countries relative to that of the United States has been stagnant for decades." 

Chart type: multi-series line chart.

X-axis: years 1970 to 2022.
Y-axis: "Share of US GNI per capita (%)" with tick marks from 0 to 60 in increments of 5.

Legend/series:
- Dark line: "Middle-income countries"
- Orange line: "Middle-income countries, excluding China"
- Light gray comparison lines labeled in the plot: "Korea, Rep.", "Poland", and "Chile"

Visible relationships/trends:
- The two aggregate middle-income-country series stay low relative to the United States, generally around the low single digits to about 8% over the period, with a modest rise after roughly 2008 and a slight easing after the mid-2010s.
- The "excluding China" series tracks slightly below the full middle-income-country series for most of the period.
- Korea, Rep. rises strongly from the mid-teens in the 1970s to just above 50% in the late 2010s/early 2020s, then remains near that level.
- Poland rises from around 10% in 1970 to the mid-20% range by 2022.
- Chile rises from roughly the low-to-mid teens in the late 1970s/1980s to about 20%+ by 2022.

Source: WDR 2024 team using data from WDI (World Development Indicators) (Data Catalog), World Bank, Washington, DC, https://datacatalog.worldbank.org/search/dataset/0037712.

Note: The plotted lines indicate the trend of average income per capita in middle-income countries and in middle-income countries, excluding China, relative to income per capita of the United States (considered the economic frontier country). Country definitions are based on the first World Development Report (World Bank 1978), in which low-income countries have gross national income (GNI) per capita of US$250 or less; middle-income countries have GNI per capita of more than US$250; and industrialized (high-income) countries consist of member countries of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, except for Greece, Portugal, Spain, and Türkiye, which are classified as middle-income countries.

Growth is expected to slow down as countries approach the economic frontier (United States). Scatter/line chart with x-axis: "GDP per capita relative to the frontier (United States) (%)" from 0 to 100, and y-axis: "Annual growth in GDP per capita (%)" from 0 to 7. The figure shows multiple country trajectories connecting projected recent-history points, with a legend for Argentina, Bangladesh, Bulgaria, Chile, China, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Poland, and Türkiye. Solid lines indicate countries that will experience convergence to the frontier over 2023–2100; dashed lines indicate countries that will experience divergence from the frontier over 2023–2100, although they were closer to the frontier in 2022. Visible patterns: Poland is a long solid teal line extending from roughly the mid-20s percent of US GDP per capita to 100%, with growth easing from a little above 5% to about 3.3–3.8%; China is a solid orange-red line extending from roughly the low-20s to the low-60s, with growth around 5% falling to around 2–3%; India is a solid brown/orange line around the low single digits to the mid-20s, flattening near 3.8%; Bangladesh is a solid olive line from very low frontier proximity to the high-20s, falling from above 6% toward about 3%; Indonesia is a solid blue line from the high single digits to the high-20s, settling near 3%; Türkiye is a solid gray line from the mid-20s to low-30s, near 2%; Argentina, Chile, Mexico, and Bulgaria are dashed trajectories rising from low frontier proximity into the mid-teens to low-20s while growth rises sharply from near 0–1% to around 1.5–3%. Source: WDR 2024 team. Note: Projections are based on extrapolation of recent historical trends using the World Bank’s Long Term Growth Model. GDP = gross domestic product.

Line chart titled: "In the Republic of Korea, Poland, and Chile, the rapid growth from middle- to high-income status has been interspersed with economic crises." X-axis: years 1960 to 2022 (tick marks shown at regular intervals, labels rotated). Y-axis: "GNI per capita (constant 2015 US$)" from 0 to 35,000. Three country series are shown: Korea, Rep. (dark blue/black line) rising from about 1,000 in 1960 to about 32,000 in 2022, with a noticeable dip/slowdown around the late 1990s and then continued growth; Poland (orange line) starting around 3,000 in 1960, rising gradually with a dip in the early 1980s, then increasing to about 13,000–14,000 by 2022 with a small dip around 2020; Chile (teal line) visible from the mid-1990s onward, rising from about 5,500 to about 16,500 by 2022, with a slight dip around 2020. Three dotted horizontal income-threshold reference lines are labeled within the plot: "LMIC threshold" near the bottom, "UMIC threshold" around the mid-lower range, and "HIC threshold" around the upper-middle range. Country names are printed near the right ends of the corresponding lines. Source note below the chart: "Source: WDR 2024 team using WDI (World Development Indicators) (Data Catalog), World Bank, Washington, DC, https://datacatalog.worldbank.org/search/dataset/0037712." Note: "GNI = gross national income; HIC = high-income country; LMIC = lower-middle-income country; UMIC = upper-middle-income country."

Figure O.1
Title: "Income per capita of middle-income countries relative to that of the United States has been stagnant for decades." 

Chart type: multi-series line chart.

X-axis: years 1970 to 2022.
Y-axis: "Share of US GNI per capita (%)" with tick marks from 0 to 60 in increments of 5.

Legend/series:
- Dark line: "Middle-income countries"
- Orange line: "Middle-income countries, excluding China"
- Light gray comparison lines labeled in the plot: "Korea, Rep.", "Poland", and "Chile"

Visible relationships/trends:
- The two aggregate middle-income-country series stay low relative to the United States, generally around the low single digits to about 8% over the period, with a modest rise after roughly 2008 and a slight easing after the mid-2010s.
- The "excluding China" series tracks slightly below the full middle-income-country series for most of the period.
- Korea, Rep. rises strongly from the mid-teens in the 1970s to just above 50% in the late 2010s/early 2020s, then remains near that level.
- Poland rises from around 10% in 1970 to the mid-20% range by 2022.
- Chile rises from roughly the low-to-mid teens in the late 1970s/1980s to about 20%+ by 2022.

Source: WDR 2024 team using data from WDI (World Development Indicators) (Data Catalog), World Bank, Washington, DC, https://datacatalog.worldbank.org/search/dataset/0037712.

Note: The plotted lines indicate the trend of average income per capita in middle-income countries and in middle-income countries, excluding China, relative to income per capita of the United States (considered the economic frontier country). Country definitions are based on the first World Development Report (World Bank 1978), in which low-income countries have gross national income (GNI) per capita of US$250 or less; middle-income countries have GNI per capita of more than US$250; and industrialized (high-income) countries consist of member countries of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, except for Greece, Portugal, Spain, and Türkiye, which are classified as middle-income countries.

Scatter plot showing economies’ GNI per capita in 1990 (x-axis) versus 2022 (y-axis), both in current US dollars. Title: “A handful of economies have transitioned from middle-income to high-income status over the last three decades.” The plot covers x from 0 to 10,000 and y from 0 to 45,000, with light horizontal gridlines and labeled income-group bands. Blue vertical threshold lines mark 1990 income-class cutoffs at US$610 (transition to lower-middle-income), US$2,465 (transition to upper-middle-income), and US$7,620 (transition to high-income). The labeled points show substantial upward movement for a small set of economies, with MAC highest near 2022 GNI per capita of about US$45,000 and 1990 GNI per capita around US$9,000; KOR is near US$36,000 in 2022 and about US$6,500 in 1990; MLT and SVN are above US$30,000 in 2022; and several economies cluster around the upper-middle/high-income boundary. Figure 1.5
Growth is expected to slow down as countries approach the economic frontier (United States). Scatter/line chart with x-axis: "GDP per capita relative to the frontier (United States) (%)" from 0 to 100, and y-axis: "Annual growth in GDP per capita (%)" from 0 to 7. The figure shows multiple country trajectories connecting projected recent-history points, with a legend for Argentina, Bangladesh, Bulgaria, Chile, China, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Poland, and Türkiye. Solid lines indicate countries that will experience convergence to the frontier over 2023–2100; dashed lines indicate countries that will experience divergence from the frontier over 2023–2100, although they were closer to the frontier in 2022. Visible patterns: Poland is a long solid teal line extending from roughly the mid-20s percent of US GDP per capita to 100%, with growth easing from a little above 5% to about 3.3–3.8%; China is a solid orange-red line extending from roughly the low-20s to the low-60s, with growth around 5% falling to around 2–3%; India is a solid brown/orange line around the low single digits to the mid-20s, flattening near 3.8%; Bangladesh is a solid olive line from very low frontier proximity to the high-20s, falling from above 6% toward about 3%; Indonesia is a solid blue line from the high single digits to the high-20s, settling near 3%; Türkiye is a solid gray line from the mid-20s to low-30s, near 2%; Argentina, Chile, Mexico, and Bulgaria are dashed trajectories rising from low frontier proximity into the mid-teens to low-20s while growth rises sharply from near 0–1% to around 1.5–3%. Source: WDR 2024 team. Note: Projections are based on extrapolation of recent historical trends using the World Bank’s Long Term Growth Model. GDP = gross domestic product.
